changes.before: If count starts at 10, what is its final value?
changes.after: Use an atomic increment so a single counter update cannot be split apart.

before: AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet performs one atomic increment and returns the updated value. Atomic operations avoid a lost update for this single counter; they do not automatically make a sequence of multiple calls one transaction.

Two workers increment the same AtomicInteger. Joins bound the task lifetime before the final get. No ordering of individual worker execution or performance improvement is promised.

new AtomicInteger() starts at zero. count.get() takes no arguments and atomically returns the current int without changing it.

The one-int constructor chooses an explicit initial value instead. No worker has run in this separate example:
```java
var initial = new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger(10);
System.out.println(initial.get());
```
Output: 10.
Expected output or behavior: 1000. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Contrast one atomic increment with a separate get followed by set. You may trace it without a JDK; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: An atomic operation acts as one indivisible step to other threads. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet safely adds one and returns the new value. It prevents lost updates for this increment. Several separate calls do not automatically become one atomic operation together.

new AtomicInteger() starts at zero; its one-int constructor sets a chosen starting value. Both workers update the same counter. After both joins finish, get reads the final value without changing it. The workers may take turns in any order.
The program prints 1000. Each worker adds one five hundred times, starting from zero.
The quiz uses new AtomicInteger(10). The workers perform the same additions on top of that starting value.

after: Keep the starting value, then add both workers' contributions.

before.question: If count starts at 10, what is its final value?
choices: 1000 because atomic updates reset the initial value
before.explanation: The 1000 atomic increments add to the initial ten.

after.question: Start count at 10 instead. What is its final value?
choices: 1000, because atomic increments reset the starting value.
after.explanation: The two workers add a total of one thousand to the starting ten, giving 1010.
